title: Year 4: year close
hook: the summit sit, looking back over a year that kept asking questions, from a king in a forest to a hymn that wonders who really knows

segments.voice: Yesterday, the summit sit, for the last time: the regional traditions, and what each place carries, from palm leaves to walnuts. Did you hand one small thing on? Today, the whole year at once. Day one thousand four hundred twenty-five.

Who really knows? The hymn of creation in the Rig Veda asks it near its end, and then, in paraphrase, it says this about the one who watches over everything from the highest heaven: perhaps he knows, or perhaps he does not know. That hymn stands in the scripture, question and all. And looking back from the top of year four, the question doesn't sit alone. This whole year kept stopping at questions. Today is the year close, and the summit sit looks at all of it by the questions it asked.
screen: `WHO REALLY KNOWS?` → `PERHAPS HE DOES NOT KNOW.` → `A YEAR OF QUESTIONS.`

segments.voice: It opened with one. A king who'd lost his kingdom and a merchant thrown out by his family asked a sage: we know these things have left us, so why doesn't knowing help? The whole Devi Mahatmya is the answer. Then the questions got sharper. The schools of thought asked how anyone knows anything at all, and the path let each school answer in its own way, ranking none. The Nyaya Sutra, near its opening, names the means of knowing. The Vedas asked, in their own voice: what covered it, where, in whose keeping? Then the women came, and several of them were remembered for a question. Gargi asked Yajnavalkya what the world is woven on, and when he told her to stop, she came back with two more. Maitreyi asked what she'd do with wealth that can't make her immortal. Damayanti found her husband by sending out a question only he would understand. Even the regions brought one: a Kashmiri teacher, Abhinavagupta, asking why a sad play leaves its audience lighter. Now turn it. A tradition could have smoothed these over and kept only the answers. This one kept the questions inside its sacred texts, in the king's mouth, in Gargi's, in a Vedic hymn. And some of them are never closed. The hymn of creation doesn't resolve its last line. It ends on perhaps. So that's the shape of year four from the top. The goddess, Shiva, the schools, the three paths, the Vedas, Ayurveda as a lens, the women, the regions. And running through them, people asking honest questions, out loud, and the tradition keeping them.
screen: `IT OPENED WITH ONE QUESTION.` · `THE SCHOOLS ASKED HOW WE KNOW.` · `GARGI, MAITREYI, DAMAYANTI ASKED.` · `THE QUESTIONS WERE KEPT.` · then, large: `IT ENDS ON PERHAPS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit with one open question. Settle, and let the breath find its own pace. Let one real question rise, something you don't know the answer to, about your life, or about God, or about anything. Don't try to answer it. Just let it sit beside you, the way the hymn lets its last line sit. Each time the mind starts building an answer, come back to the breath, and to the question, still open. If you pray, you can hold it before God, or the goddess, as it is. The bell holds the time.
Year four. The goddess, Shiva, the schools of thought, the Vedas, the women and the regions, looked at from the top by the questions they asked. Today's word.

Your line: Year 4, year close. Today, ask someone one honest question, and let them answer without hurrying them. Tomorrow, the last day of the year, and the ranges ahead. Day one thousand four hundred twenty-five.

howItsDone: Hindu traditions keep questions inside their texts: the Upanishads hold dialogues between teachers and questioners, and the hymn of creation, with its open last line, is chanted as part of the Rig Veda.

myth: the hymn of creation ends with a confident answer
it ends on perhaps: perhaps he knows, or perhaps he does not know.
Gargi stops asking for good once Yajnavalkya warns her
she comes back later with two more questions.
this year let each school of thought answer in its own way
the schools were taught side by side, and none was ranked.

fork.setup: you're compiling a sacred collection. one hymn about creation ends by wondering whether even the one in the highest heaven knows. what do you do with it?
options: keep it, and chant it with the rest.
fork.reveal: the hymn was kept in the Rig Veda, open last line and all, and is still chanted.

original.note: Vedic Sanskrit: ko addhā veda, who really knows? from the hymn of creation, Rig Veda 10.129.

trapdoor: what you thought: a year of religious study is a year of answers.
what it means: year four kept stopping at questions, and the tradition kept them in its texts.
what a scholar hears: Rig Veda 10.129, the Nasadiya Sukta, closing on 'or perhaps he does not know', and the Brihadaranyaka's questioners like Gargi and Maitreyi.
